transcript.content: Hello, and welcome. I'm Dr. [Name], a psychiatrist. What brings you in to see me today?

Well, I'm here because... honestly, it's been going on for nearly two years now. I am absolutely sure the contractor we hired, along with some of the people on my block, have been quietly working together to cheat us. They are keeping my kitchen half-wrong on purpose. It's just so frustrating. My husband keeps showing me receipts and telling me it's fine, and the contractor always has some excuse, but I know what's really happening. 

You know, it reminds me of when we first moved into this neighborhood back in the late 80s. The block association was so different then. We used to have these lovely summer block parties—everyone would bring a dish. I always made my famous potato salad. People would ask for the recipe, but I never gave it out. It was my mother's recipe, actually. She grew up in a time when you really had to stretch a dollar, so she knew how to make simple things taste wonderful. She had this old ceramic bowl she always mixed it in... I think my sister has that bowl now. Anyway, what was I saying? Oh, right, the kitchen. Yes, they're definitely doing it on purpose, no matter what anyone says.
Have you ever heard voices or seen things that other people around you couldn't hear or see?

Voices? No, no, nothing like that. I'm not crazy, Doctor. My hearing is perfectly fine. Well, I did have to get my ears checked last year at Dr. Miller's office. He’s the ear doctor down on 4th Street. Such a nice man, he always wears these brightly colored bowties. I think his wife makes them for him. She owns that little fabric shop near the old post office... I went in there once looking for some yellow gingham to make curtains for the kitchen window. This was before the contractor started ruining the room, of course. Yellow is just such a cheerful color, don't you think? My grandmother had a yellow kitchen, and it always felt so warm when the sun came in. 

But anyway... what were you asking me? Oh, about seeing things. No, I don't see anything that isn't there either. I just need my reading glasses for the morning paper, that's all.

When your husband shows you the receipts and tells you the kitchen is fine, do you think he might actually be right, or are you completely certain that the contractor and your neighbors are working together to cheat you?

Oh, he's definitely not right. I am completely certain about it. I mean, it’s been nearly two years now of them quietly working together to cheat us, keeping my kitchen half-wrong on purpose. He can wave all the receipts he wants in my face, and that contractor can give me a million excuses, but I know what I know. 

My husband, bless his heart, he just trusts every piece of paper you hand him. He’s always been like that, ever since he worked at the hardware store downtown before they closed. He used to manage the inventory there, keeping all these little paper ledgers. He had a special green pen he only used for the end-of-month totals. You can't even find pens like that anymore, the ones with the really fine felt tips. I tried to buy one for my crossword puzzles last month at the pharmacy, but they just had those cheap ballpoints that smudge everywhere. I do the Sunday puzzle every week, usually with a cup of Earl Grey tea... it's a nice little routine. I use a little bit of honey instead of sugar, it's better for your throat. 

But anyway, yes, the kitchen. I don't care what his receipts say or what he thinks. I am absolutely sure the contractor and those neighbors are in on it together to ruin my kitchen.

Is it physically possible for a contractor and your neighbors to work together secretly to keep your kitchen half-wrong on purpose, or does that seem like something that couldn't actually happen in the real world?

Well, of course it's possible! They're doing it right now, aren't they? It's not like they're building a spaceship, they're just... they're just messing with the cabinets and the plumbing. Anyone can do that if they're sneaky enough. 

Speaking of sneaky, you know who was sneaky? That cat we had when I was a girl. Barnaby, we called him. He was a tuxedo cat, mostly black with these little white paws that looked like mittens. He figured out how to open the pantry door. My mother couldn't understand how the bread bags kept getting torn open. We blamed my brother for weeks! My brother, he was always eating. He's a tall man now, lives out in Ohio. Sells insurance, I think. Or maybe it's real estate? He sends a card every Christmas, always with one of those long, typed letters folded inside about his golf trips. I don't play golf myself. Too much walking in the hot sun. I prefer gardening, though my knees aren't what they used to be. I used to grow the most beautiful hydrangeas... 

But, yes, it's completely possible. They're doing it, and I know they're doing it, no matter how impossible it sounds to anyone else.

If I told you that I've spoken with your contractor and your neighbors, and they all say they're not working together to cheat you, would you consider that it's at least possible you might be mistaken about this?

Mistaken? No, Doctor, I'm not mistaken. Of course they told you that! They're not going to just confess to you. Like I said, for nearly two years now I’ve been sure the contractor and some people on my block have been quietly working together to cheat us. They're keeping my kitchen half-wrong on purpose, and it doesn't matter how many receipts my husband shows me or how many excuses they give. They lie just as easily as breathing. 

Speaking of lying, did I ever tell you about my sister-in-law, Martha? Oh, she could tell a fib with a straight face. She once told the whole family she was a strict vegetarian, but I caught her eating a hot dog behind the pavilion at the Fourth of July picnic! It was one of those jumbo franks, too, with the mustard just dripping down her chin. We always used to go to Centennial Park for the Fourth. They had a lovely fireworks display over the lake. I haven't been to the lake in years, though. The water gets so murky in the late summer, all that green algae... it smells a bit like boiled cabbage when the wind blows. I make a wonderful stuffed cabbage, by the way. The trick is to put just a pinch of brown sugar in the tomato sauce. It cuts the acidity perfectly. My mother taught me that when I was just a teenager... 

But... oh, what was I saying? Yes, the contractor and the neighbors. No, I wouldn't consider being mistaken. They're just lying to you, Doctor, same as they lie to me.

You mentioned they're keeping your kitchen half-wrong on purpose by working together secretly. In your view, is there something physically impossible or against the laws of nature about what they're doing, or is it just something that would be difficult or require them to be sneaky?

Laws of nature? Heavens no, it's nothing like magic or anything impossible. It's just... well, it just takes them being incredibly sneaky when no one is looking. 

I never really understood the laws of nature or physics anyway, to be honest. I took a science class in high school with Mr. Henderson. He had this terrible comb-over that would flap in the breeze whenever he opened the classroom window. We always wanted the window open because the radiators in that old building ran so terribly hot. They clanked, too. Just *clank, clank, clank* all winter long. 

My husband tried to bleed our radiators at the house last November, but he used the wrong little key and got rusty water all over the hallway runner. Such a shame, it was a lovely Persian rug, a wedding gift from my Aunt Clara. She had terrible taste in men but absolutely wonderful taste in textiles. She actually married a man who sold vacuum cleaners door-to-door, if you can believe it. He used to demonstrate them by throwing dirt right on people's living room carpets... 

Anyway, what was I saying? Oh, right. No, it's not impossible at all. Just very, very sneaky.

When you say they're keeping your kitchen half-wrong on purpose, do you mean they're doing something that goes against the laws of nature or the way the world works, or is it something that's just very difficult to do without being caught?

Well, like I just said, it's not against the laws of nature. It's just very difficult to pull off without getting caught, which is why they have to be so sneaky about it. They wait until my husband is at the hardware store, or when I'm out back tending to the garden. 

Speaking of the garden, I noticed the most peculiar thing this morning. The neighbor's dog—a golden retriever, lovely temperament but completely untrained—dug a hole right near my prize rose bushes. I spent all of April pruning those bushes. Pruning is an art, really. You have to cut at just the right angle above the bud. My grandmother taught me that. She had a sprawling garden in Connecticut. We used to spend our summers there. We'd take the train up from the city, and the conductor always had a pocket watch on a gold chain. He'd let my brother listen to it tick. My brother loved trains. Still does, actually. He has a whole model train setup in his basement in Ohio. The little towns he builds around the tracks are so detailed, they even have tiny street lamps that light up. 

But, yes, to answer your question, it's not impossible. It's just very hard to do, and they are very, very good at being sneaky.

When you say they're keeping your kitchen half-wrong on purpose, what specific evidence do you have that proves they're working together? Can you describe the actual things you've observed that show this conspiracy?

Well, the evidence is everywhere if you just open your eyes, Doctor. Like I said, I've been sure for nearly two years now that the contractor and some of the people on my block are quietly working together to cheat us. They keep the kitchen half-wrong on purpose. And my husband, bless his heart, he keeps showing me receipts and telling me it's just delays, and they give him all these excuses about supply chains. But I see how they look at each other. 

My husband has always been entirely too trusting, though. He bought a used car back in 1982 from a man who swore it had only been driven to church on Sundays. Turned out the transmission was held together with duct tape and a prayer. We broke down on the side of the highway during a terrible thunderstorm. The rain was coming down so hard the windshield wipers couldn't keep up. I remember I was wearing my favorite silk blouse, a lovely emerald green color. You can't just throw silk in the washing machine, you know, it ruins the fibers. You have to hand wash it with a gentle detergent, or take it to a dry cleaner. There used to be a wonderful dry cleaner on Elm Street, run by a Greek family. They always smelled like fresh linen and lavender. I love the smell of lavender. I keep little sachets of it in my dresser drawers to keep the moths away. Moths are such a nuisance, aren't they? They ruined a beautiful wool sweater of mine last winter. 

But anyway... yes, the kitchen. They just keep it half-wrong on purpose, and no matter how many receipts my husband waves in my face or what excuses the contractor gives, I know they're working together to cheat us. It's been going on for two years.

When you think about the contractor and your neighbors working together to keep your kitchen half-wrong on purpose, do you believe they have some kind of special power or ability that regular people don't have, or are they just using normal human abilities to do this?

Special powers? Oh, heavens no. I don't think they're mind readers or superheroes or anything silly like that. They're just regular, everyday people using normal abilities to be incredibly deceitful. 

I don't really believe in anyone having special powers, to be honest. Although, my sister-in-law Brenda used to swear up and down she had "the gift of sight." She would insist on reading everyone's tea leaves after Sunday dinner. We always drank Earl Grey, the loose-leaf kind, not those little paper bags. She bought it from a specialty shop downtown. The man who ran it was so dapper, he always wore a velvet bowtie. You just don't see men dressing up like that anymore, do you? It's all sweatpants and those terrible rubber shoes with the holes in them now. 

My nephew wore a pair of those rubber shoes to a nice restaurant last Easter, bright orange ones too. His mother was absolutely mortified, but she couldn't get him to take them off. He’s a very stubborn boy. He plays the trombone, though, and he’s quite good at it. We went to his winter concert at the middle school, and the band director was waving his arms so wildly I thought he might take flight right there off the stage. 

But anyway, what were we talking about? Oh, the neighbors and the contractor. No, no magic powers at all. They're just normal people who are very, very good at sneaking around behind my back.

When you think about the contractor and neighbors keeping your kitchen half-wrong on purpose, do you think they might be using some kind of hidden technology or surveillance equipment to coordinate their actions, or are they just coordinating in normal ways like phone calls and meetings?

Hidden technology? Oh, I don't know anything about that. I haven't seen any cameras or microphones or anything like you see in those spy movies. I imagine they just use their cell phones like everyone else these days to coordinate it all. People are always glued to those little screens, aren't they? 

My granddaughter got one of those smartphones for her twelfth birthday. Twelve! Can you imagine? When I was twelve, we had a heavy yellow rotary phone attached to the kitchen wall with a curly cord that stretched all the way into the dining room. My mother used to get so aggravated with me because I'd pull the cord as far as it would go just so I could sit under the dining table and talk to my best friend, Susan. 

Susan's family actually still had a party line for a few years, and sometimes if you were quiet, you could hear Mrs. Gable from down the street breathing on the other end. She was a bit of a busybody, but Mrs. Gable made the most wonderful peach cobbler. She brought it to the church potluck every single August. The church didn't have air conditioning back then, just these big ceiling fans that did nothing but push the hot air around, so we'd all sit in the pews fanning ourselves with the Sunday programs. The paper they used for those programs was so thick, almost like cardboard, with a lovely textured edge. 

But anyway, what was I saying? Oh, right. No, I haven't noticed any secret gadgets or surveillance equipment. Just normal phone calls and whispering behind my back, I'm sure.

If you were to imagine for a moment that you might be wrong about the contractor and neighbors working together—even though you're quite sure you're right—what do you think might explain why your kitchen looks the way it does?

Well, I suppose... if I were to imagine I was wrong—which I'm not, Doctor, I've been telling you, I've been sure for nearly two years now that the contractor and those people on my block are quietly working together to cheat us and keep my kitchen half-wrong on purpose. But if I had to pretend... I don't know, maybe I'd say it was just bad luck or terrible workmanship? My husband keeps showing me all those receipts and giving me their excuses about backorders and supply issues. 

He keeps all his receipts in this old metal lockbox he bought at a garage sale. It's an olive green color, very military looking. He got it from a man who used to collect antique radios. My father had an antique radio, a beautiful wooden Zenith model that sat in the corner of the living room. We used to listen to it on Sunday evenings. The wood was polished so brightly you could almost see your reflection in it. My mother used lemon oil on it every week. Lemon oil smells so wonderful, doesn't it? Much better than that chemical smell in the aerosol cans they sell now. I tried one of those aerosol dusting sprays once, and it made me sneeze for an hour straight. My allergies have been terrible this year anyway, with all the pollen. The oak trees in our front yard have been dropping those little yellow stringy things everywhere. They get stuck to the bottom of your shoes and track all over the house. I have a lovely cream-colored rug in the entryway, and it is just a nightmare to keep clean. 

But no matter what my husband says or how many receipts he pulls out of that green box, I know what's really happening. They're keeping it half-wrong on purpose. I'm not wrong about that.

You've mentioned your husband shows you receipts and the contractor gives excuses about supply chains and delays. If that's all true—the receipts, the delays, the supply issues—is it possible that the kitchen really is just taking longer than expected, and that there's no conspiracy at all?

Well, I know my husband thinks that. He really does. He looks at those receipts and he listens to their little speeches about backorders, and he just nods along. But... no, it's not possible. I've been telling you, I've known for nearly two years now that they are quietly working together—the contractor and those people on my block—just to cheat us and keep the kitchen half-wrong on purpose. It doesn't matter how many excuses they give. 

My husband is just too trusting. He’s always been that way, bless his heart. When we first got married, he bought a used car from a man who promised it ran perfectly. A Ford Pinto, it was. Pea green. We hadn't even driven it five miles off the lot before the muffler completely fell off and started dragging on the pavement, making the most awful racket. Sparks were flying everywhere! We had to pull over at a diner, one of those classic ones with the shiny silver outside and the red vinyl booths inside. 

I always loved sitting in those booths. They served the most incredible milkshakes there, served in those tall glass fountains with the extra metal tin on the side. My favorite was strawberry, but only if they used real strawberries, not that artificial syrup that tastes like medicine. The pharmacist down at the corner drugstore, Mr. Higgins, he used to give out cherry lollipops that tasted exactly like that artificial syrup. He was a very tall man, Mr. Higgins. He had to duck every time he walked through the door to the back room where they kept the prescriptions. 

But no, to answer your question... it's not just taking longer. They're doing it on purpose, no matter what those receipts say. I'm absolutely certain of it.

Looking back over everything we've discussed today, do you think there's any chance at all that your belief about the contractor and neighbors working together might not be real, or are you completely certain this is actually happening?

Doctor, I know we've been going over this, but there is absolutely no chance it's not real. I've been completely sure for nearly two years now. The contractor and those neighbors on my block are quietly working together to cheat us, keeping that kitchen half-wrong on purpose. And it doesn't matter how many of those little receipts my husband pulls out of his box or how many excuses they give me. I know what I know. 

Just like I know the grout they used is the wrong shade. It's beige instead of eggshell. You know, my sister Linda painted her entire first apartment beige. This was back in Chicago, right near the lake. The wind coming off Lake Michigan in November is just bone-chilling. We went up to visit her for Thanksgiving one year, and I had to wear two pairs of wool socks just to keep my toes from going numb when we walked to the grocery store. Linda knitted those socks herself. She was always so crafty. She made this beautiful afghan for my first baby, all pastel yellow and mint green. 

Mint green used to be so popular in the seventies, especially for bathrooms. We had a mint green sink and a matching bathtub in our first house. The bathroom had one of those fuzzy rug sets, you know, the ones that go around the base of the toilet and over the lid? I always thought the lid covers were a bit unhygienic, to be honest. You have to wash them constantly, and they take absolutely forever to dry. Our old dryer used to make a terrible thumping sound if you put anything too heavy in it, like towels or rugs. It would shake the whole laundry room floor. 

But anyway, what was the question? Oh, am I certain. Yes, I am completely certain this is actually happening with the kitchen. There's no doubt in my mind at all.

If a doctor you trusted completely examined all the work in your kitchen and told you there was nothing wrong with it, would you believe them, or would you still believe the contractor and neighbors are working together to keep it wrong?

Well, if a doctor I really trusted came to look at it... I mean, a doctor isn't a contractor, are they? But I suppose... well, the most trusted doctor I ever had was Dr. Aris. He delivered both my boys. He had the gentlest voice and he always wore these wonderful silk ties with little mallard ducks on them. My husband tried to wear silk ties when he was still working, but he’d always spill coffee on them by nine in the morning. He worked at the insurance company downtown, you know, the building with the big glass atrium? They had a cafeteria there that served the most awful meatloaf. It tasted like wet cardboard mixed with ketchup. I make a wonderful meatloaf, if I do say so myself. I use a mix of ground beef and pork, and a little dash of Worcestershire sauce. That's the secret, really. You have to let it bake slowly in a good, working oven. 

Which I would do, if my kitchen wasn't ruined. So to answer you, no, even if Dr. Aris himself came back from the grave and looked at it, I wouldn't believe him if he said it was fine. Because I've been completely sure for nearly two years now. The contractor and some of those people on my block are quietly working together to cheat us. They are keeping my kitchen half-wrong on purpose, and I won't be convinced otherwise, no matter how many excuses they give or how many of those receipts my husband tries to show me. I just know what's happening.

Besides the kitchen and the contractor and your neighbors, do you notice other people in your daily life—people at the store, on the street, people you see on television—do anything that seems like they're sending you messages or communicating about you in some way?

No, I don't think anyone else is sending me messages. It's just the contractor and those neighbors on my block. The people at the store are just doing their jobs. Speaking of the store, I went to the grocery store yesterday to pick up some of those little mandarin oranges, you know, the ones that come in the wooden crates? They used to come in wooden crates when I was a girl. My father would buy a whole crate of them at Christmastime. We'd keep them in the root cellar so they'd stay cold. 

Our root cellar smelled so earthy, like wet soil and old potatoes. My brother Thomas used to hide down there when he didn't want to do his chores. He was always trying to get out of weeding the garden. We had a huge vegetable garden. Tomatoes, cucumbers, zucchini... oh, the zucchini would just take over if you weren't careful! My mother would make zucchini bread, zucchini boats, fried zucchini... we'd eat it until we were sick of it. She used this old, heavy cast iron skillet for frying. You had to season it just right with oil, or everything would stick. 

My husband tried to wash that skillet with soap once, early in our marriage. I thought my mother was going to have a heart attack when she found out. You never use soap on cast iron, everyone knows that. But he didn't know any better. He grew up in the city, you see. They ordered takeout a lot. Chinese food, mostly. I love a good egg roll, but only if the cabbage inside is still a little bit crunchy. If it's too mushy, it ruins the whole thing. 

But anyway, no, nobody on the television or at the store is sending me messages. It's just the kitchen situation.

When you see the contractor and your neighbors together, or when you notice them looking at each other, do you think they're specifically communicating about you and your kitchen, or do you think they might be communicating about other things in general?

Well, when I see them together, they are definitely communicating about me and my kitchen. I see them giving each other those looks, you know, the ones where they think I don't notice. It's so obvious they're plotting about keeping it half-wrong. 

Speaking of looks, my neighbor across the street, Mrs. Gable, gives the most awful looks when people don't mow their lawns on time. She has this pristine, manicured lawn. I swear she must be out there with nail clippers trimming the edges. She used to have these beautiful pink flamingos in her yard, the plastic ones? They were so retro. I love retro things. I found this amazing vintage Pyrex bowl at a garage sale last summer. It's that classic primary yellow color. Pyrex is just so sturdy. You can drop it and it won't even chip. 

I remember dropping a glass once when I was little, right in the middle of the kitchen floor. It shattered everywhere. My father was furious, not because I broke the glass, but because I didn't sweep it up properly and he stepped on a tiny sliver later that night. He was wearing his favorite slippers, too. They were plaid, red and black. He loved plaid. He had a plaid thermos he took to work every single day. Filled it with black coffee. I can't drink black coffee, it's far too bitter. I need at least two sugars and a splash of cream. Real cream, not that powdered nonsense. 

But yes, to answer your question, when I see the contractor and those neighbors, they are absolutely communicating about me and my kitchen. There's no question about it.

When you're out in public—at the grocery store, or walking down the street—do you ever notice strangers or people you don't know doing things that seem like they're trying to send you a message or let you know they're aware of your kitchen situation?

No, heavens no. Strangers out in public aren't doing anything like that. When I'm walking down the street or at the store, people are just minding their own business. 

Speaking of walking down the street, I just bought the most comfortable pair of walking shoes. They're white with these little navy blue stripes on the side. My podiatrist recommended them because I have a slight arch issue. His office is right next to that little bakery on Elm Street, the one with the green awning? Oh, they make the most divine lemon meringue pie. The meringue is just miles high, perfectly toasted on top. My grandmother used to make lemon meringue pie from scratch, but she lived in Florida and had her own lemon tree right in the backyard. 

We visited her once in July and the humidity was just unbearable. I thought I was going to melt right into the driveway. You know they say you can fry an egg on the sidewalk when it gets that hot? My Uncle Arthur actually tried it once. He just cracked a grade-A large egg right onto the concrete. It didn't really fry, it just made a sticky mess, and then a flock of seagulls came down and made an absolute racket fighting over it. He was always doing silly things like that. He bought a metal detector from a catalog and spent a whole summer looking for pirate gold at the beach... 

But anyway, no, I don't notice strangers sending me any messages or letting me know they know about the kitchen. It's really just the contractor and those specific neighbors I told you about.

When you're at home or out and about, do you ever notice things in your surroundings—like the way someone parks their car, or a song playing on the radio, or the clothes someone is wearing—that feel like they're somehow connected to you or meant as a sign about what's happening with your kitchen?

No, no, I don't see signs in things like that. Cars and clothes and the radio... they're just normal things. 

Though, speaking of the radio, I was listening to this oldies station the other day while I was dusting the living room. They played that song, you know, "Tie a Yellow Ribbon Round the Ole Oak Tree"? I haven't heard that in ages! My sister Brenda used to play that record over and over until I thought I'd lose my mind. She had this little portable record player, the kind that folded up like a suitcase. It was powder blue. We shared a bedroom, and she would sit on her bed—she had the bed by the window—and just play it on a loop. 

She loved the window bed because she could look out at the streetlamp. The streetlamp would buzz, this low hum, especially when it rained. We lived on a corner lot, so we got all the traffic noise, too. The milkman used to come so early, his bottles clinking together in that wire carrier. Clink, clink, clink. He was a very nice man, Mr. Henderson. Always wore a crisp white uniform, even in the dead of winter. I don't know how he kept it so clean with all the slush and snow. 

Snow was different back then. It felt like it piled up to the roof! My father would have to shovel a path just so we could get to the front gate. He had this big metal snow shovel that he kept in the garage right next to his tools. He was very particular about his tools. Every wrench had its place on the pegboard, outlined in black marker so you knew exactly where it belonged. 

But, oh, what were you asking? Right, signs and things. No, I don't notice anything like that. Just the contractor and the neighbors, like I said.

Well, I'm here because... honestly, it's been going on for nearly two years now. I am absolutely sure the contractor we hired, along with some of the people on my block, have been quietly working together to cheat us. They are keeping my kitchen half-wrong on purpose. It's just so frustrating. My husband keeps showing me receipts and telling me it's fine, and the contractor always has some excuse, but I know what's really happening. 

You know, it reminds me of when we first moved into this neighborhood back in the late 80s. The block association was so different then. We used to have these lovely summer block parties—everyone would bring a dish. I always made my famous potato salad. People would ask for the recipe, but I never gave it out. It was my mother's recipe, actually. She grew up in a time when you really had to stretch a dollar, so she knew how to make simple things taste wonderful. She had this old ceramic bowl she always mixed it in... I think my sister has that bowl now. Anyway, what was I saying? Oh, right, the kitchen. Yes, they're definitely doing it on purpose, no matter what anyone says.

Which I would do, if my kitchen wasn't ruined. So to answer you, no, even if Dr. Aris himself came back from the grave and looked at it, I wouldn't believe him if he said it was fine. Because I've been completely sure for nearly two years now. The contractor and some of those people on my block are quietly working together to cheat us. They are keeping my kitchen half-wrong on purpose, and I won't be convinced otherwise, no matter how many excuses they give or how many of those receipts my husband tries to show me. I just know what's happening.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the patient's belief system includes ideas of reference (F22.9 - Unspecified Delusional Disorder) or is confined to a circumscribed delusional theme (F22.0 - Erotomanic type, or other specified delusional disorder). Specifically, I need to assess whether the patient believes other people are communicating about her or sending her special messages/signs, or if the delusion is limited to the kitchen conspiracy.
doctor.question: Besides the kitchen and the contractor and your neighbors, do you notice other people in your daily life—people at the store, on the street, people you see on television—do anything that seems like they're sending you messages or communicating about you in some way?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about ideas of reference or delusions of reference (people on TV, on the street sending messages). My profile only includes delusions about the contractor/neighbors, functioning, functional impairment, and duration. It does not include ideas of reference or other types of delusions.

patient.answer:
No, I don't think anyone else is sending me messages. It's just the contractor and those neighbors on my block. The people at the store are just doing their jobs. Speaking of the store, I went to the grocery store yesterday to pick up some of those little mandarin oranges, you know, the ones that come in the wooden crates? They used to come in wooden crates when I was a girl. My father would buy a whole crate of them at Christmastime. We'd keep them in the root cellar so they'd stay cold. 

Our root cellar smelled so earthy, like wet soil and old potatoes. My brother Thomas used to hide down there when he didn't want to do his chores. He was always trying to get out of weeding the garden. We had a huge vegetable garden. Tomatoes, cucumbers, zucchini... oh, the zucchini would just take over if you weren't careful! My mother would make zucchini bread, zucchini boats, fried zucchini... we'd eat it until we were sick of it. She used this old, heavy cast iron skillet for frying. You had to season it just right with oil, or everything would stick. 

My husband tried to wash that skillet with soap once, early in our marriage. I thought my mother was going to have a heart attack when she found out. You never use soap on cast iron, everyone knows that. But he didn't know any better. He grew up in the city, you see. They ordered takeout a lot. Chinese food, mostly. I love a good egg roll, but only if the cabbage inside is still a little bit crunchy. If it's too mushy, it ruins the whole thing. 

But anyway, no, nobody on the television or at the store is sending me messages. It's just the kitchen situation.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the patient has ideas of reference (F22.9 - Unspecified delusional disorder) or specific persecutory delusions (F22.0 - Erotomanic type, or more accurately persecutory type). I need to clarify if the patient believes others are communicating about her specifically through their actions, or if the delusion is solely focused on the conspiracy against her kitchen/finances.
doctor.question: When you see the contractor and your neighbors together, or when you notice them looking at each other, do you think they're specifically communicating about you and your kitchen, or do you think they might be communicating about other things in general?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about ideas of reference/delusions of reference specifically regarding the contractor and neighbors (whether they are communicating about the patient or about general things). My symptom profile covers the fixed belief that they are working together to cheat her (S019), but does not specifically address whether their general interactions are perceived as ideas of reference/communicating about her. S019 was already used to describe the core delusion.

patient.answer:
Well, when I see them together, they are definitely communicating about me and my kitchen. I see them giving each other those looks, you know, the ones where they think I don't notice. It's so obvious they're plotting about keeping it half-wrong. 

Speaking of looks, my neighbor across the street, Mrs. Gable, gives the most awful looks when people don't mow their lawns on time. She has this pristine, manicured lawn. I swear she must be out there with nail clippers trimming the edges. She used to have these beautiful pink flamingos in her yard, the plastic ones? They were so retro. I love retro things. I found this amazing vintage Pyrex bowl at a garage sale last summer. It's that classic primary yellow color. Pyrex is just so sturdy. You can drop it and it won't even chip. 

I remember dropping a glass once when I was little, right in the middle of the kitchen floor. It shattered everywhere. My father was furious, not because I broke the glass, but because I didn't sweep it up properly and he stepped on a tiny sliver later that night. He was wearing his favorite slippers, too. They were plaid, red and black. He loved plaid. He had a plaid thermos he took to work every single day. Filled it with black coffee. I can't drink black coffee, it's far too bitter. I need at least two sugars and a splash of cream. Real cream, not that powdered nonsense. 

But yes, to answer your question, when I see the contractor and those neighbors, they are absolutely communicating about me and my kitchen. There's no question about it.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient has ideas of reference (beliefs that neutral events are specifically directed at them) versus a more circumscribed delusional system. F22.0 (paranoid type) typically involves persecutory delusions with ideas of reference, while F22.9 (unspecified) may have more limited delusional content. I need to clarify whether the patient believes OTHER people's actions and communications are directed at her specifically, or if she only focuses on the contractor and neighbors' conspiracy.
doctor.question: When you're out in public—at the grocery store, or walking down the street—do you ever notice strangers or people you don't know doing things that seem like they're trying to send you a message or let you know they're aware of your kitchen situation?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about ideas of reference/delusions of reference involving strangers in public places. The symptom profile does not contain a specific item for delusions of reference or strangers sending messages (it only has the primary delusion about the contractor/neighbors, functioning, functional impairment, and duration).

patient.answer:
No, heavens no. Strangers out in public aren't doing anything like that. When I'm walking down the street or at the store, people are just minding their own business. 

Speaking of walking down the street, I just bought the most comfortable pair of walking shoes. They're white with these little navy blue stripes on the side. My podiatrist recommended them because I have a slight arch issue. His office is right next to that little bakery on Elm Street, the one with the green awning? Oh, they make the most divine lemon meringue pie. The meringue is just miles high, perfectly toasted on top. My grandmother used to make lemon meringue pie from scratch, but she lived in Florida and had her own lemon tree right in the backyard. 

We visited her once in July and the humidity was just unbearable. I thought I was going to melt right into the driveway. You know they say you can fry an egg on the sidewalk when it gets that hot? My Uncle Arthur actually tried it once. He just cracked a grade-A large egg right onto the concrete. It didn't really fry, it just made a sticky mess, and then a flock of seagulls came down and made an absolute racket fighting over it. He was always doing silly things like that. He bought a metal detector from a catalog and spent a whole summer looking for pirate gold at the beach... 

But anyway, no, I don't notice strangers sending me any messages or letting me know they know about the kitchen. It's really just the contractor and those specific neighbors I told you about.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the patient has ideas of reference (belief that neutral events/people are communicating about her) versus a circumscribed delusional belief limited to the kitchen/contractor situation, which would help differentiate F22.0 (Delusional Disorder, somatic type) from F22.9 (Delusional Disorder, unspecified)
doctor.question: When you're at home or out and about, do you ever notice things in your surroundings—like the way someone parks their car, or a song playing on the radio, or the clothes someone is wearing—that feel like they're somehow connected to you or meant as a sign about what's happening with your kitchen?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about delusions of reference (e.g., finding personal meaning or signs in random environmental stimuli like cars, radio songs, clothes), which is not part of the patient's symptom profile.

patient.answer:
No, no, I don't see signs in things like that. Cars and clothes and the radio... they're just normal things. 

Though, speaking of the radio, I was listening to this oldies station the other day while I was dusting the living room. They played that song, you know, "Tie a Yellow Ribbon Round the Ole Oak Tree"? I haven't heard that in ages! My sister Brenda used to play that record over and over until I thought I'd lose my mind. She had this little portable record player, the kind that folded up like a suitcase. It was powder blue. We shared a bedroom, and she would sit on her bed—she had the bed by the window—and just play it on a loop. 

She loved the window bed because she could look out at the streetlamp. The streetlamp would buzz, this low hum, especially when it rained. We lived on a corner lot, so we got all the traffic noise, too. The milkman used to come so early, his bottles clinking together in that wire carrier. Clink, clink, clink. He was a very nice man, Mr. Henderson. Always wore a crisp white uniform, even in the dead of winter. I don't know how he kept it so clean with all the slush and snow. 

Snow was different back then. It felt like it piled up to the roof! My father would have to shovel a path just so we could get to the front gate. He had this big metal snow shovel that he kept in the garage right next to his tools. He was very particular about his tools. Every wrench had its place on the pegboard, outlined in black marker so you knew exactly where it belonged. 

But, oh, what were you asking? Right, signs and things. No, I don't notice anything like that. Just the contractor and the neighbors, like I said.

inference.note: Patient demonstrates a persistent, fixed false belief (nearly 2 years) about contractor and neighbors conspiring to ruin kitchen. Belief is held with absolute conviction despite contradictory evidence (receipts, contractor explanations, husband's reassurance). Patient explicitly denies hallucinations, delusions of reference, ideas of persecution beyond the kitchen situation, and magical thinking. The delusion is non-bizarre (conspiracy is physically possible, just requires deception). No evidence of mood disorder or organic cause. This is consistent with Delusional Disorder, Persecutory Type (F22.0). F22.9 (unspecified delusional disorder) is less appropriate given the clear persecutory content.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient presents with a non-bizarre delusion of a conspiracy involving the contractor and neighbors working together to deliberately keep her kitchen 'half-wrong on purpose' for nearly two years. She maintains absolute certainty despite contradictory evidence (receipts, contractor explanations, husband's reassurance). She explicitly denies hallucinations, ideas of reference from strangers/media, magical thinking, or special surveillance technology. The delusion is circumscribed to this single theme without extension to other domains. She demonstrates intact reality testing in other areas and no evidence of mood disorder, psychotic symptoms beyond the delusion, or significant cognitive decline. The persistent, non-bizarre, encapsulated nature of the delusion over approximately 2 years meets criteria for Delusional Disorder, Persecutory Type (F22.0).
